source_text: Nec in uno hoc aut alio fuit ista dignatio. Namque Aemilianus, quamuis equestris ordinis gentiliter haberetur, unus tamen in carcere et ipse de fratribus, qui ad quinquagesimum prope aetatis annum carnis continentia puer uenerat, continuatis in carcere gemina superpositione ieiuniis et orationibus saepe repetitis, per quas deuota mens pasta in alium diem sacramento domini parabatur, in somno die medio reclinatus, mox quiete discussa talia nobis suae uisionis arcana patefecit. Producto mihi, inquit, e carcere homo gentilis, hoc est frater meus carnalis, occurrit. In res nostras admodum curiosus insultabunda uoce perquirit, sciscitans quatenus nos in illis poenalibus tenebris et inedia carceris haberemur. Cui responsum dedi, milites Christi et in tenebris clarissimam lucem et in ieiunio cibum saturabilem dei habere sermonem. Et cum haec audisset, Scitote, inquit, quod omnes uos qui in carcere habemini, si obnixe perstabitis, manebit poena capitalis. At ego qui uerebar ne conpositum luderet fraude mendacium, confirmare uotum meum uolui et Vere, inquam, patiemur omnes? At ille rursus affirmat: Gladius uobis et sanguis in proximo est. Sed uelim scire, inquit, an omnibus uobis, qui uitam istam contempnitis, indiscreta et aequalia munerum caelestium praemia rependantur. Cui responsum dedi: Non sum idoneus huius tam magnae rei ferre sententiam. Attolle, inquam, oculos paulisper ad caelum: iam uidebis innumerabilem turbam micantium siderum. Numquid stella omnis pari luminis honore praefulget? Et tamen lumen omnibus unum est. Ad haec ille curiosius iterum quod interrogaret inuenit. Ergo si qua discretio est, inquit, qui uestrum sunt in promerenda domini uoluntate potiores? Nimirum, inquam, prae ceteris duo, quorum nec tibi dicenda et deo nota sunt nomina. Nouissime incumbenti acrius et perscrutanti molestius, Ii sunt, inquam, qui quo difficilius et tardius uincunt, gloriosius coronantur; et propter hoc scriptum est: Facilius intrabit camelus per foramen acus, quam diues in regna caelorum.
pass_a_gloss: Nor was that gracious condescension in this one man or in another. For Aemilianus, although he was reckoned in pagan manner as of equestrian rank, yet himself one in prison from among the brethren, who had come as a boy with continence of flesh to nearly the fiftieth year of age, with fasts prolonged in prison by a double superpositio and with prayers often repeated, by which the fed devout mind was being prepared for another day by the sacrament of the Lord, reclined in sleep at midday, and soon with sleep shaken off disclosed to us such secrets of his vision. 'When I had been brought out,' he says, 'from prison a pagan man met me, that is my brother according to the flesh. Very curious about our affairs he inquires with mocking voice, asking how we were faring in those penal darknesses and in the hunger of prison. To him I gave answer that soldiers of Christ have both in darkness a most bright light and in fasting a satisfying food, the word of God. And when he heard this, Know, he says, that all you who are held in prison, if you persist obstinately, capital punishment will remain. But I, who feared lest he sportingly played a lie composed with deceit, wished to confirm my desire and said, Shall we truly all suffer? And he again asserts: Sword and blood are near at hand for you. But I would like to know, he says, whether to all of you who despise this life indiscriminate and equal rewards of heavenly gifts are repaid. To him I gave answer: I am not fit to pass judgment on so great a matter. Lift, I say, your eyes a little to heaven: now you will see the countless crowd of glittering stars. Does every star shine with equal honor of light? And yet the light is one to all. At this he again more curiously found what to ask. If then there is any distinction, he says, who of you are foremost in meriting the Lord's will? Namely, I say, before the rest two, whose names are both not to be told to you and known to God. At last, as he pressed more keenly and probed more importunately, They are, I say, those who the more difficultly and slowly they conquer, the more gloriously are crowned; and on this account it is written: More easily will a camel enter through the eye of a needle than a rich man into the kingdoms of heaven.
pass_b_english: Nor was that gracious favor confined to this one man or to another. For Aemilianus, though reckoned after the pagan fashion as of equestrian rank, was himself one of the brethren in prison, who as a boy had kept his flesh in continence almost to his fiftieth year, and in prison he prolonged his fasts, doubling them and laying one upon another, and with prayers often repeated, by which his devout mind, fed and nourished, was made ready for the next day by the sacrament of the Lord. At midday he lay back in sleep, and presently, shaking off his rest, he laid open to us the secrets of his vision in this manner. When I had been brought out of prison, he said, a pagan man met me, that is, my brother after the flesh. Exceedingly curious about our affairs, he questioned me in a mocking voice, asking how we fared in that punishing darkness and in the hunger of prison. I answered him that the soldiers of Christ possess in darkness a most radiant light, and in fasting a satisfying food, the word of God. When he heard this he said: Know that all of you who are held in prison, if you persist resolutely, will face capital punishment. But I, fearing lest he were playing a fabricated lie for a fraud, wished to confirm what I longed for, and I said: Shall we truly all suffer? And he affirmed again: Sword and blood are close upon you.

Then he said: But I would like to know whether to all of you who despise this present life the rewards of heavenly gifts are repaid without distinction and as equals. I answered him: I am not fit to pass sentence on so great a matter. Lift your eyes a little to heaven: now you will see the countless throng of glittering stars. Does every star shine with equal honor of light? And yet the light is one to all. At this he still more inquisitively found another question to ask. If then there is any distinction, he said, who among you are foremost in meriting the Lord's will? I said: Surely two before the rest, whose names are both not to be told to you and are known to God. At last, as he pressed more sharply and probed more importunately, I said: They are those who, the more difficultly and slowly they conquer, are crowned the more gloriously; and therefore it is written: More easily will a camel pass through the eye of a needle than a rich man enter into the kingdoms of heaven (Matthew 19:24).
